uas_topic: Privacy/surveillance, bodily-injury-fear conduct, and contraband delivery (incl. to correctional/detention facilities)
regulated_activity: Surveillance of a person in a private place; operation placing another in reasonable fear of bodily injury; delivery of contraband
summary: Makes it a crime to use a UAS intentionally or knowingly to: (1) conduct surveillance of another person in a 'private place' (a place where a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy) — summary offense, up to $300 fine; (2) operate in a manner placing another person in reasonable fear of bodily injury — summary offense; or (3) deliver, provide, transmit, or furnish contraband in violation of 18 Pa.C.S. §5123 or 61 Pa.C.S. §5902 (which cover contraband into a correctional or mental health institution and county/municipal detention facilities) — felony of the second degree. 'Surveillance' is defined as using a UAS to observe, record, or invade the privacy of another.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Standard survey/mapping/inspection flight paths over commercial, industrial, or public infrastructure sites are unlikely to implicate the 'private place' surveillance provision, but keep camera angles and loiter time away from residential yards, windows, and other areas with an expectation of privacy during any corridor or site-documentation flight. Route flight paths to keep clear standoff from any correctional or detention facility given the felony-level contraband-delivery provision, even though delivery isn't the intent — proximity alone can raise questions worth avoiding.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Because 'private place' and 'reasonable fear of bodily injury' are judgment-based standards with only a $300 summary penalty for the first two prongs, the practical legal risk is lower than in states with felony-level general surveillance statutes — but document flight purpose and altitude near residential areas as a matter of good practice. Treat the correctional/detention-facility contraband provision as a bright line requiring advance coordination for any project genuinely needing to fly near such a facility.

summary: Provides that 18 Pa.C.S. §3505 preempts and supersedes any municipal ordinance, resolution, rule, or other enactment regulating the ownership or operation of UAS; as of the section's effective date, a municipality may not regulate UAS ownership or operation unless expressly authorized by statute. source_title: Drone use to locate, drive, harass, or take game or wildlife
citation: 34 Pa.C.S. § 2308; implementing regulations at 58 Pa. Code Ch. 141
regulated_activity: Using a drone to locate, drive, harass, or take game or wildlife, including recovery of downed/wounded game
aec_relevance: Moderate (context for State Game Lands work)
summary: Prohibits using a drone to locate, drive, harass, or take any game or wildlife. The Game Commission interprets this to cover tracking or recovery of wounded or downed deer as part of the act of hunting — drone-assisted deer recovery is currently not legal in Pennsylvania, and hunters have been cited (fines up to $2,500, potential loss of hunting privileges) for using drones this way. Senate Bill 303 (2025-2026 session) would carve out a recovery exception but has not been enacted.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or corridor-survey flights on or near State Game Lands, plan flight paths and altitude to avoid any appearance of pursuing, driving, or harassing wildlife — steady survey-pattern flights at planned altitude are the safest posture, and avoid any recovery-adjacent framing in field communications given how strictly the Commission has enforced the recovery interpretation.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document flight purpose (survey/mapping, not wildlife-related) for any AEC work on State Game Lands, and monitor SB 303's status since a recovery exception would not by itself broaden this statute's application to commercial survey work, which was never within its scope.

uas_topic: State forest UAS operation — generally permitted
regulated_party: UAS operators in PA State Forests
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS on state forest land
requirement_type: Generally permitted, subject to general forest-use rules
permit_or_approval_required: No permit for general/recreational operation; commercial operation requires prior contact with the local forest district office and a written Commercial Activities Agreement (CAA), plus proof of a remote pilot certificate and registered aircraft available on request
summary: Unlike the state park default prohibition, DCNR's state forest drone policy generally allows UAS operation on Pennsylvania's 2.2 million acres of state forest land across 20 forest districts, subject to specific operational conditions set out in DCNR's own published policy document: fly below 400 ft AGL; no launch, landing, or operation in designated Natural and Wild Areas or other posted-closed areas (UAS are treated as both "motorized equipment" and "mechanical transport" for this purpose); no flight within an active FAA Temporary Flight Restriction; do not fly over or within 100 meters (328 ft) of wildlife, and do not approach animals vertically; maintain visual line of sight; stay at least 5 miles from an airport or backcountry airstrip; and a maximum aircraft weight of 55 lbs. Recreational flight is recommended (not required) to be confirmed with the local forest district office in advance; commercial operation requires contacting the forest district office first and obtaining a written Commercial Activities Agreement (CAA), with a remote pilot certificate and registered aircraft available on request.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: State forest land is a comparatively easier launch/land environment than state parks for timber, environmental-monitoring, or corridor-survey work, but treat the Commercial Activities Agreement (CAA) requirement as a real precondition, not a formality -- contact the specific forest district office before mobilizing, keep the flight under 400 ft AGL and 5 miles from any airport, and route around designated Natural and Wild Areas and any active TFR (e.g., a nearby wildfire).
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the specific forest district office for the property before scheduling any commercial UAS work; request the current Commercial Activities Agreement (CAA) form, lead time, and any district-specific conditions, and have remote pilot certification and aircraft registration on hand -- the policy states these must be available on request.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the executed Commercial Activities Agreement (CAA) in the project file for any commercial state-forest UAS work; the policy's operational conditions (Natural/Wild Area avoidance, TFR compliance, 100-meter wildlife buffer, 5-mile airport buffer, 55 lb weight limit) are DCNR's own stated terms, not merely aspirational guidance, and should be treated as compliance requirements for the engagement.
